headline: French Student Protests Escalate Amid Education Crisis

sources.excerpt: French student unions vowed on Friday to keep up protests after scoring what they called their first win in a campaign that is increasingly supported by Paris' elite universities, with 141 schools still shut around the country. The protests have snowballed into a wider movement, with more university students weighing in to express their anger over what they call a dysfunctional system, worsened by spending cuts spurred by France's budget crunch. Student and teacher unions have called for another round of nationwide school strikes next Tuesday. France's education ministry is in the process of urgently contacting around 3,000 spare teachers who could be sent to schools with the most pressing needs, often located in low-income areas, Education Minister Edouard Geffray said. Speaking during a visit to a school in the Paris region that was vandalised during protests, he said more than 100 teaching staff had been injured so far in the nationwide protests. The movement has fueled similar student protests in Belgium, which on Friday were amplified by a national strike during which scuffles broke out between protesters and police in Brussels. Police cleared a blockade at Assas university, a top French law school in central Paris, on Friday morning. Nearby, elite engineering school Mines Paris was also disrupted by blockades. The Institut Catholique, a private university known for being particularly conservative, said on its website it would switch to remote classes due to a blockade of its campus. Student unions meanwhile hailed what they see as their first real win, after the government late on Thursday pledged to send some 3,000 teachers, who are fully qualified but have not yet started work, to fill staffing gaps, one of the protesters' main grievances. The move, which the government called an "emergency plan", shows it is worthwhile for students to continue their protests, Marius Mesnil, from a high school student union, told Franceinfo radio. "I find it crazy we need to block hundreds of high schools just to get a vacancy plan," he added. The measure is effective immediately and will cost "several dozen million euros", Geffray told broadcaster TF1 late on Thursday. Three weeks into the protest, President Emmanuel Macron's government is struggling to work out how to balance demands for more education spending with the need to rein in public debt. Investors are closely watching the government's next moves in a highly indebted country where street anger has often been tamed with more state spending. This time, France's large pension outlays and its need to rein in public spending leave little room for manoeuvre. Stephane Boujnah, the head of Euronext, which runs the Paris stock market, said Paris urgently needed to make tough choices. "What sacrifice are we asking of our own children? ... maybe we need to spend a little less on pensions so that we have a little more money for the children," he told RMC radio. Nearly 10% of teaching hours are unstaffed at French state high schools, according to education ministry figures, prompting a growing number of wealthier parents to abandon the public sector in favour of private schooling, a trend that some experts say will only reinforce social inequality. "Let's be frank, families are leaving public schools for our institutions," said Pierre-Vincent Gueret, who heads France's federation of Catholic private schools. The interior ministry said 71,500 people took to the streets in Paris and elsewhere on Thursday. While most protests were peaceful, violence flared up in some places. In Belgium, meanwhile, students joined demonstrations alongside striking workers as the country's two largest labour unions staged a national strike on Friday, disrupting public transport, air travel and other sectors. Thousands of people marched through central Brussels in a protest that was largely peaceful, although some scuffles broke out with police, who used tear gas and water cannons in some instances. One banner carried by student protesters read: "I skipped class to defend class."

Among the hundreds of thousands of people who took to the streets in France on Tuesday were Paolina and Violette, eighteen and seventeen years old, arguing politely with a white-haired man sucking apple juice from a juice box. The two young women carried signs: “EVEN PEDOPHILES don’t FUCK US as much as THE EDUCATION DEPARTMENT” declared one, handwritten in ink a few shades darker than Paolina’s blueberry-colored manicure. “FOUR RIOT POLICE FOR ONE STUDENT / ONE PROFESSOR FOR THIRTY-FIVE.” Paolina is studying fine arts at the Sorbonne Nouvelle; Violette is a communications major at the Institut Universitaire de Technologie. They had come out to the Place de la République, in Paris, to protest the conditions at French schools. The familiar scent of grilling merguez wafted through the air as Violette began to enumerate the system’s failures. “This year, the government eliminated four thousand teaching positions,” she said. (Her stats were dead-on.) The man, who declined to give his name, thought that the problems facing French schools could be resolved quite easily: all the authorities had to do was “put more A.I.” into the curriculum. “That’s not something that interests me, in an intellectual sense or in a moral sense,” Paolina shot back. “Prompting ChatGPT? I think I know how to do it better already than professors who are forty-five years old and hardly know how to use the technology.” The man accepted defeat and slunk off, slurping, toward the Boulevard du Temple. The protests began on September 17th, at a single high school, Lycée Saint-Exupéry, in the Parisian suburb of Créteil. Students and teachers had grown tired of not having a nurse or a deputy head teacher, dealing with leaks and clogged toilets, and trying to concentrate in un-air-conditioned classrooms, where the temperature could soar to more than a hundred degrees in summer. They decided to do something about it, erecting a blocus, or “blockade,” at the entrance to the school, mostly with trash cans. A few days later, some students launched explosive devices into the school lounge, injuring two people. Nobody at “Saint-Ex” expected that the blocus would spread across the country, but social media did its work, awakening in French students a determination to make themselves heard after years of diminished means and accumulating problems—and providing, for their detractors, a pretext for blaming the country’s ills on febrile, feckless adolescents. Two weeks in, students at some six hundred and forty lycées and thirty universities across forty cities have joined the movement, drawing in adults as well, including many of their parents and teachers; elected officials, mostly from the left and the far-left; and trade unions like the powerful C.G.T. The demonstrations have been met with aggressive and often outrageous policing. Around seven thousand protesters, most of them minors, have been arrested. During Tuesday’s march alone, officers arrested around two hundred more people than they did on the day the gilets jaunes sacked the Arc de Triomphe, in 2018. Protesters have sometimes resorted to violence, too, and they have set fire to or otherwise damaged at least twenty-four schools. But the majority of students have been peaceful, and many come off in interviews as almost freakishly mature. “What we have is a classic lycéen movement, using routine blockade methods, that speak of the conditions they’re facing,” the sociologist Sebastian Roché observed, on Radio France. “They constitute a threat to the government, because it’s weak, but not to the Republic.” In northern France, a police officer threw a tear-gas grenade directly into a fourteen-year-old’s face and shattered his jaw. Another child picked up a stun grenade that the police had launched and lost a hand. In May of 1968, student protesters imagined a future of poetic discovery—“Sous les pavés, la plage!” (“Under the pavement, the beach!”) their famous slogan went. In the Gen Z revolt that some students have labelled “May ‘six seven,’ ” their rallying cries are more direct. “MACRON, FUCK YOUR PROF, NOT OURS,” with its brutal jab at the President’s marriage to his former drama teacher, is emerging as a favorite line, along with “TOO YOUNG TO BE LISTENED TO / OLD ENOUGH TO BE TEAR-GASSED” and, deliciously, “BISMILLAH, C’EST LES TENÈBRES,” quoting an undercover cop’s rumored attempt to pose as a protester on Snapchat using what he thought sounded like youth slang. The sociologist Paolo Stuppia, a co-author of “The Geopolitics of Youth: Engagement and (De)mobilization,” explained that previous major student movements—such as a 2006 uprising prompted by a law that allowed employers to fire workers under twenty-six without cause—centered on opposition to specific policies. This time, with the French government under severe fiscal pressure and straining to fund public services, students are “making offensive claims, not just defensive claims,” he said. Their demands are extremely clear. They want repairs to insalubrious buildings (rats, roaches, puddles), reduced class sizes (France has the largest in Europe, with seventy per cent of lycée classes counting more than thirty students), and the hiring of more teachers (middle- and high-school students lost as many as twenty million class hours last year, owing to staff shortages). They want a shorter, more efficient school day. They want an overhaul of Parcoursup, a widely loathed college-admissions system, introduced in 2018. Their concerns have failed to impress certain observers, such as the center-right deputy Philippe Juvin, who recently declared that they should “get back to work,” like “their little friends in China.” Are the students just “slackers,” as Marion Maréchal—a French member of the European Parliament and the far-right leader Marine Le Pen’s even harder-right niece—put it? Is the movement the result of “out of control mass migration” and “Islam,” as Donald Trump claimed, in a particularly unfounded bit of racist refrigerator poetry? Most French people don’t think so. According to a poll commissioned by Le Figaro, some sixty-two per cent believe that the students’ actions are justified. In Bordeaux, farmers showed up at the barricades with breakfast—bread, jam, and apple juice. (“Only terroir products,” one volunteer boasted.) In the Tenth Arrondissement of Paris, near the Canal Saint-Martin, a mural appeared, seemingly overnight, depicting the lycéens as heroic revolutionaries in a style that seemed equal parts Delacroix and Dragon Ball.
